person.name: Dong Hwi Kim
person.affiliation: Mechanical Engineering & Electrical and Computer Engineering · Seoul National University
person.intro: I am an undergraduate at Seoul National University, double majoring in Mechanical Engineering and Electrical and Computer Engineering. I work at the intersection of robotics, 3D vision, and machine learning.
person.bio: I am an undergraduate researcher in the RPM Robotics Lab with Prof. Ayoung Kim and the AIDAS Lab with Prof. Jaeyoung Do. My current work focuses on 3D Gaussian Splatting for SLAM and visual data augmentation for robot learning.

research.title: 3D Gaussian Splatting for SLAM
research.image_alt: Conceptual illustration of camera observations, Gaussian scene representation, and camera trajectory; not an experimental result
research.summary: Investigating 3D Gaussian Splatting for simultaneous localization and mapping. A manuscript is currently in preparation.
research.role: Ongoing research on 3DGS-based SLAM; manuscript in preparation.

sections.heading: Research direction
sections.body: This ongoing project investigates the use of 3D Gaussian Splatting in simultaneous localization and mapping. The goal is to connect camera motion estimation with a 3D representation of the surrounding scene.

sections.heading: Current status
sections.body: The manuscript is in preparation. Further method details, experimental results, and publication information will be shared as the work progresses.

research.title: 3DGS Data Augmentation for Robot Learning
research.image_alt: An FR3 manipulation episode rendered from three camera viewpoints using Gaussian scene assets
research.summary: Building the 3DGS augmentation module for a larger robotic dataset effort: metric scene alignment, articulated robot rendering, and measurable quality gates for generated demonstrations.
research.role: Responsible for the 3DGS data augmentation module within a larger collaborative dataset project.

sections.heading: My scope within the collaboration
sections.body: I am responsible for the 3D Gaussian Splatting augmentation module in a broader robotic dataset collaboration. The module turns workcell captures and demonstrations into reusable, reposable scene assets and synchronized training views. The broader collaboration and manuscript remain in progress.

sections.heading: A good render is not enough
sections.body: A scene can look convincing and still have the wrong metric scale. The pipeline uses ChArUco calibration and pose-invariant lengths between rigid robot parts to check scale against the URDF. Registration is then refined using high-opacity Gaussian cores with scale held fixed. This avoids letting a diffuse reconstruction shell determine the robot’s dimensions.

sections.heading: Connecting appearance to kinematics
sections.body: Gaussians are assigned to the nearest CAD link surface, and inverse forward kinematics converts posed robot geometry into reusable link assets. Forward kinematics then reposes them along a demonstration. Object attachment and release use an explicit kinematic contract, so appearance, joint motion, and object motion share a defined coordinate relationship.

sections.heading: Repairing capture-specific failure modes
sections.body: Static captures miss cube bottoms, and a low-texture tabletop can reconstruct as haze. The pipeline merges only missing cube geometry from a rolled capture and replaces tabletop fog with a sheet on the calibrated plane, bounded by the measured table footprint. These are targeted scene repairs, not an assumption that novel-view quality alone guarantees usable manipulation geometry.

sections.heading: Validation before dataset generation
sections.body: The module checks geometry, forward-kinematics round trips, grasp state, object-pose continuity, wrist-camera visibility, and black frames before accepting generated episodes. Resumable stages and immutable dataset shards separate long generation jobs from release validation. The engineering focus is to turn visible rendering defects into measurable acceptance criteria; dataset-generation checks do not by themselves establish downstream policy success.

projects.title: Autonomous Perception for the SNU AI Robot Challenge
projects.image_alt: Team 7's autonomous mecanum-wheel robot in the competition arena
projects.summary: An autonomous mecanum robot built around the realities of collection, braking, and on-board perception. My work focused on perception and model training for the team’s second-place competition system.
projects.role: Perception and model training, together with Jinyong Jun.

sections.heading: The engineering problem
sections.body: The robot had 180 seconds to find, collect, and deliver two target classes announced at match time. A Jetson Orin Nano ran perception and navigation on a four-wheel mecanum chassis. The key mechanical constraint was a passive, three-object basket: driving forward captured an object, while reversing released it. That made motion planning, stopping, and perception part of the same collection problem.

sections.heading: From software commands to wheel motion
sections.body: The Jetson sent body-velocity commands over a 115200-baud USB serial link to an ESP32, which commanded four JGB37-520 geared DC motors through DRV8871 drivers. The host interface explicitly converted its forward/right/yaw convention to the chassis axes and reapplied per-wheel feed-forward and encoder-direction calibration after connecting. Motion commands carried a duration and auto-stopped at the controller. The hot path sent commands without waiting for an acknowledgement, avoiding serial round-trip delays in the control loop.

sections.heading: Control choices driven by the mechanism
sections.body: The team used a fixed sweep route with live collection decisions. LiDAR wall fitting supplied pose; an IMU integrated yaw to terminate calibrated turn pulses. Lateral moves used LiDAR feedback by default because the documented timed-strafe calibration left 4–7 cm error. Stops used a calibrated reverse-braking pulse, with a useful speed range around 42–57 cm/s. Cruise was therefore set near 44 cm/s rather than pushed toward the motor limit. Route corrections also had to respect the basket’s tendency to release its load during backward travel.

sections.heading: My focus: perception that navigation can use
sections.body: I worked on perception and model training with Jinyong Jun. Two outward-angled USB cameras let the system observe objects beside the route without stopping to face them. The YOLO instance-segmentation node combined both cameras into one UDP message and reprojected horizontal detections into a common forward-facing bearing. Navigation then applied confidence, range-normalized mask-area, bearing, and grid-cell ownership gates. This separated visual evidence from the decision to collect a target.

sections.heading: What the integration makes clear
sections.body: A detector’s offline accuracy is only one part of a usable robot. At the documented scan speed, an object could appear in only two or three inference frames, so demanding many repeated detections could reject real targets. The repository includes an Orin benchmark for model latency and a frame-freeze check for each camera. The engineering lesson is to choose the model, observation gates, and vehicle speed together, and to debug raw camera frames alongside motion logs.

sections.heading: Competition validation
sections.body: Team 7 finished second with 140/200 points across two final runs, collecting three shape targets and two fruit targets per run. These are team-level system results; my contribution was perception and model training. The repository also records calibration limits, rather than presenting the competition prototype as a fully general navigation system.

projects.title: Accelerated MRI Reconstruction
projects.image_alt: Team MRI reconstruction framework using brain and knee experts with Feature VarNet and FI VarNet
projects.summary: A reconstruction pipeline that combines MRI measurement consistency, anatomy-specific models, and practical GPU-memory and checkpoint management for 4×/8× accelerated scans.

sections.heading: Reconstructing measurements, not just sharpening images
sections.body: The input is undersampled multi-coil k-space, so plausible appearance alone is insufficient: a reconstruction must remain tied to the acquired measurements. The Feature VarNet and FI VarNet implementations estimate coil sensitivities and combine learned updates with data-consistency operations. FI VarNet also includes image-domain cascades. The design couples a learned image prior to the MRI acquisition model.

sections.heading: Specialization with explicit routing
sections.body: Brain and knee scans, and 4× and 8× sampling, present different reconstruction conditions. The team trained specialized experts instead of relying on one shared checkpoint for every input. In the inference code, routing is deterministic: coil count identifies the anatomy and the sampling mask determines acceleration. This is an explicit expert-selection pipeline, rather than a learned gating network.

sections.heading: Making the training pipeline practical
sections.body: The repository provides DeepSpeed-based training, activation-checkpointing configuration, resumable checkpoints, and conversion of distributed checkpoint state into FP32 model weights. MRI-aware augmentation and a warmup/cosine schedule support training. These pieces matter because a useful reconstruction architecture must also fit the available memory and survive interrupted experiments.

sections.heading: Two different forms of averaging
sections.body: Checkpoint averaging combines compatible parameter tensors into one model; prediction ensembling instead executes separate models and averages their reconstructions. The averaging utility checks parameter names and shapes, while the inference path supports expert-specific model pairs. Keeping these mechanisms separate makes the inference-cost trade-off explicit: weight averaging does not add another model forward pass.

sections.heading: Result and engineering takeaway
sections.body: Team 2rm1000, with Jinseok Choi, placed third and received a KRW 2,500,000 team prize. The project demonstrates a complete path from measurement-aware models to specialized inference and reusable checkpoints. Competition placement is the reported validation here.

projects.title: Structured Scene Reordering with Multimodal LLMs
projects.image_alt: Diagram of mapping frame-order views into a common coordinate system for Random4 inference
projects.summary: Turning multimodal reasoning into a constrained engineering pipeline: valid permutation decoding, consistent frame coordinates, and a single averaged LoRA adapter for the official submission.

sections.heading: A structured output contract
sections.body: Given a sentence and four shuffled frames, the system must return each input frame’s chronological rank. Chronological sequence and per-input rank are inverse permutations; confusing them can invalidate an otherwise correct prediction. The implementation explicitly converts between the two representations and formats the submission through a shared utility.

sections.heading: Reasoning with a constrained decoder
sections.body: The Qwen3.5-27B model uses LoRA adaptation and structured readouts: six frame-pair comparisons and four chronological slots. Their evidence scores the 24 possible orders, and exhaustive decoding selects one valid permutation. This gives the output a useful guarantee—each frame appears exactly once—rather than depending on free-form text to obey the task schema.

sections.heading: Aggregating views in the same coordinates
sections.body: Random4 inference evaluates four input-image orderings. Before averaging raw logits, each view is mapped back to the original frame identities; otherwise the same output position would refer to different images in different views. One decoder then operates on the combined evidence. The repository tests permutation mappings and validates the final submission schema.

sections.heading: Accuracy without another inference ensemble
sections.body: The final-selected Exp43 adapter averages nine language-LoRA snapshots from the same training trajectory in CPU float32. It remains one adapter at inference, so this parameter-space averaging adds no forward passes. Temporal-gap supervision and local hard-negative ranking belong to training. Crop-based test-time augmentation is documented separately as post-competition work.

sections.heading: Result and engineering takeaway
sections.body: GeekSeek finished eighth overall. The repository records 0.91463 as the official final-selected private score; the higher late Crop-TTA score is not an official competition result. The main engineering lesson is that representation contracts, aggregation coordinates, and reproducible artifact selection are as consequential as the model choice.

projects.title: Physics-Guided Wind Power Forecasting
projects.image_alt: Zephyr Analytics team cover for the 2025 Wind Power Prediction Competition
projects.summary: Using turbine physics as a baseline, learning its residual errors, and optimizing an ensemble against both forecast accuracy and an economic settlement metric.
projects.role: Model architecture design and hyperparameter optimization.

sections.heading: Two objectives for an operational forecast
sections.body: The competition required hourly generation forecasts for Gyeongju, Yangyang, and Yeongdeok. Prediction error and settlement revenue describe different aspects of usefulness, so the project reported both. A forecast that looks numerically close must still be evaluated under the competition’s economic scoring rule.

sections.heading: Let physics explain the baseline
sections.body: The team used a physical power curve and weather-derived features, including air-density estimation informed by the Arden–Buck equation. This gives the model a physical starting point: weather conditions imply an expected generation level. A residual LightGBM model then corrects the baseline’s remaining error instead of making the entire mapping depend on a single unconstrained predictor.

sections.heading: My contribution: architecture and optimization
sections.body: I worked on model architecture design and hyperparameter optimization. The team combined the hybrid prediction with Ridge Regression and Random Forest models and used Optuna for tuning, including ensemble weights. Derrick Junsu Lee led machine learning and testing, while Hyunseung Lee handled preprocessing and feature engineering.

sections.heading: Validation and engineering takeaway
sections.body: Zephyr Analytics placed third among 270 teams, with reported NMAE of 19.34% and settlement revenue rate of 22.09%. The site-wise distributions in the evaluation slide help contextualize the aggregate result. The key design lesson is to divide the problem between a physical baseline, learned error correction, and the operational evaluation criterion. These details are drawn from the supplied team slides; no public implementation repository is linked.

projects.title: Automated Filming Device
projects.image_alt: Sunflower-inspired face-tracking camera device with a yellow phone mount and white circular base
projects.summary: A Raspberry Pi pan–tilt filming prototype that turns face-position error into servo commands, with calibrated pulse widths, manual infrared control, and a load-supporting mechanical assembly.

sections.heading: The mechanism and the control objective
sections.body: A solo creator needs the subject to stay framed while the camera moves smoothly enough to remain usable. The team combined a Raspberry Pi, a wide-view camera, two pan–tilt servos, an infrared receiver, and a ball-transfer support. The support reduces friction and distributes the assembly’s load; the two axes provide horizontal and vertical reframing.

sections.heading: From pixels to actuator commands
sections.body: The final program uses Picamera2 and OpenCV’s Haar-cascade detector, selecting the largest detected face. Its horizontal and vertical offsets from the image center are normalized by frame dimensions and converted into incremental servo-angle commands. pigpio maps those commands to servo pulse widths with an explicit offset, pulse cap, and angle limits.

sections.heading: What the controller actually implements
sections.body: The source contains proportional and derivative terms, but both derivative gains are set to zero in final.py. The checked-in implementation therefore acts as proportional image-error feedback, rather than demonstrating a tuned PID controller. The stored angle is the commanded angle; there is no separate measured joint-angle feedback in this program. This distinction separates visual feedback from the servo’s internal position regulation.

sections.heading: Manual control and device state
sections.body: A separate thread reads LIRC’s irw output so remote commands can switch automatic/manual operation, move either axis, stop, or exit while the vision loop continues. An LED indicates face detection. On shutdown, the program terminates the remote process, stops the camera, and disables servo pulses. This joins the tracking algorithm to an actual device interaction loop.

sections.heading: Result and engineering takeaway
sections.body: The team received the 2024 HD Hyundai Mechatronics Competition Grand Prize and a KRW 3,000,000 team prize. The project’s engineering value lies in connecting camera coordinates, control gains, calibrated pulse widths, mechanical support, and user input. The linked demos show prototype behavior; the repository does not supply quantitative tracking-error or settling-time measurements.

projects.title: TaXer & WaXer: Forecasting Periodic Time Series
projects.image_alt: Original presentation slide showing the TaXer periodic feature extraction and cross-attention architecture
projects.summary: Integrating periodic or dilated-convolution features into a transformer forecaster, with explicit tensor interfaces and evaluation across weather and retail time series.

sections.heading: The design question
sections.body: Can a transformer benefit from a feature extractor that explicitly captures temporal structure? The team compared TaXer, which uses TimesNet-style periodic features, with WaXer, which uses WaveNet-style dilated causal convolutions. Weather and Sticker Sales sequences provide different tests of the same integration idea.

sections.heading: Connecting two models at the right interface
sections.body: TaXer detects dominant periods through FFT-based TimesNet features, then uses a learned linear projection to match the transformer’s embedding dimension. Variable-wise patch embeddings provide the endogenous sequence, while the extracted features are broadcast as cross-attention context. The encoder’s global token queries that context. This is feature-level integration, rather than averaging two independent forecasts.

sections.heading: An alternative temporal prior
sections.body: WaXer replaces the periodic feature extractor with dilated causal convolutions while keeping the projection and transformer integration pattern. The two variants let the team compare explicit periodic structure with a convolutional receptive field. Input/output shapes and per-variable normalization are handled explicitly so forecasts can be returned at the original scale.

sections.heading: Evaluation and engineering takeaway
sections.body: The supplied report compares models on global weather, Korean weather, and Sticker Sales, including model-size ablations. Its main Sticker comparison reports TaXer MSE of 0.1569 versus 0.1647 for TimeXer. These are course-project results under the reported setup. The useful engineering question is how representation choice, model capacity, and inference cost interact.

sections.heading: Team and materials
sections.body: This SNU Introduction to Deep Learning project was completed by Donghwi Kim, Jinwoo Seo, Hyeonseop Shin, and Manyoung Han. The code, report, and presentation provide the implementation and experimental context; the work is presented as a course project.
